name: Anabolic diet / high calorie eating

lead: The Anabolic Diet is a cyclic ketogenic plan described in a 1995 book by powerlifter and writer Mauro Di Pasquale, nicknamed the Pork Chop Diet. People use it, along with other heavy-eating approaches, to eat enough to support training and gain muscle size.

It works by alternating low-carbohydrate stretches with higher-carbohydrate periods while keeping calories high, so training is fueled and mass can be added. No studies of its effect on appearance were found, and sources specific to it are limited.

paras: People follow it as a repeating weekly pattern of low-carb eating followed by higher-carb eating, alongside heavy lifting. It is usually run as a bulking phase, and size changes show up over weeks to months of consistent training and eating.

No clinical studies of the diet were found, and the sources reviewed document no risks specific to it. Like other very low-carb and very high-calorie plans, it can be hard to sustain and may not suit people with medical conditions or those on medication; a clinician can advise.

angle.text: The Anabolic Diet is a cyclic low-carb, high-calorie bodybuilding plan used to fuel hard training and push muscle gain. The route to a bigger look runs through eating enough to support training and add mass. No studies of its appearance results were found.

lead: The Anabolic Diet is a cyclic ketogenic diet (CKD) published in 1995 by Mauro Di Pasquale, and it was nicknamed the Pork Chop Diet [1]. Di Pasquale, born in 1945, is an Italian-born Canadian powerlifter and writer who won the IPF World Powerlifting Championships in 1976 and later worked as an anti-doping figure in professional wrestling [1].

Heavy or high-calorie eating more broadly refers to eating a large calorie surplus to gain weight and muscle, a practice covered under bulking [2]. No studies found test the Anabolic Diet for appearance outcomes.

paras: Di Pasquale advocates low-carbohydrate diets and wrote for the bodybuilding press; his 1995 book presents the diet as a cyclic ketogenic approach [1].

Wikipedia's bodybuilding article describes a calorie surplus as keeping muscle in an anabolic state and says larger or longer surpluses add more fat [2]. See the related entry on dirty and lean bulking.

timeline.event: Di Pasquale publishes The Anabolic Diet [1].
